items.title: George Avakian interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clinton, New York, April 21, 1998
items.q: Between us Howard Scott, who was another young producer in the Masterworks Department, and I produced the first 100 pop and 100 classical LPs

But the big thing is that having had this miniature exposure as it grew, I got exposed more and more to what was happening in the New York club scene and so forth, and recording wise I wasn’t too keen on getting into it. Well first of all you have to remember that in ‘47, a year after I got into the record business, I was not only just a junior producer of the pop singles of the day, there wasn’t any album…

albums became more and more important in Europe and finally Japan. When I left Columbia Records in 1958, Europe was bringing in almost as much money in the album sales to the American originators as the domestic sales were. And when Japan got on board, which was really about 1960 I would say, Japan ended up being bigger than Europe. Now all of this international business was made possible through the long playing record, and jazz was an important part of it. It isn’t anymore and hasn’t been for many years because…
